Design Principles

Grounded in how children actually learn.

This curriculum is designed through the lens of child development research, DLCS learning progressions, and Universal Design for Learning. Every lesson moves from concrete to abstract, exploration to creation, and individual to collaborative.

Grades K–2 — Explore and Discover

Curiosity before complexity.

Learners in grades K–2 are in the preoperational to early concrete operational stage. Every lesson prioritizes active, hands-on, sensory engagement, oral language, and guided exploration before any abstract skill is introduced. Technology is introduced as a purposeful tool — never as a replacement for physical, social experience.

Grades 3–5 — Think and Create

Problems worth solving.

Students in grades 3–5 are developmentally ready for abstract thinking, sustained collaboration, and iterative design. Lessons are structured around authentic challenges that require planning, testing, and revision. Students build real solutions, document their thinking, and present their work to genuine audiences. Cross-disciplinary connections are explicit in every unit.

Safety and Privacy

Monitored, secure, educator-directed.

Every digital activity uses only Clever-approved, school-authorized tools on monitored devices with secure logins. No student personally identifiable information is entered into any public or unmonitored space. All tools are educator curated and used to extend and reinforce the stated learning goal.

Standards Alignment

Every lesson traceable to a strand.

All lessons are aligned to the Massachusetts DLCS Learning Progression across four strands: Computing and Society (CAS), Digital Tools and Collaboration (DTC), Computational Thinking (CT), and Computer Systems (CS). Standards are cited at the lesson level with a one-sentence explanation of alignment, enabling transparent documentation and professional conversation.

Curriculum Structure

Two grade bands. Six units per band. One coherent arc.

Week
Grade Band K–2 — Explore and Discover

Building the foundations of computational thinking through curiosity, play, and guided discovery.

Instruction is grounded in Vygotsky’s zone of proximal development, Piaget’s concrete learning principles, and Universal Design for Learning. Unplugged activities precede or accompany every digital experience. All tools are Clever-approved, educator-directed, and run on monitored, secure school devices.

CTDTC
CT: Algorithms, steps, patterns, debugging, and programming [K-2.CT.b, K-2.CT.d] Standards #1-3
Today's Agenda
Welcome Routine
Greeting, settle in, review lab norms, and connect to the unit question. Review routines if needed.
Announcements
Today’s focus is What Is a Step?. We are working on concept practice for this unit.
Discovery Learning
Model a simple sequence using physical objects (blocks, cups, crayons). Students give directions to a partner to reproduce the sequence step by step.
Story Time
How to Code a Sandcastle by Josh Funk.
Stations — Explore and Hands-On
Station 0
Station 0: Story Rug / Waiting Room — no device needed. Tracing, picture sort, or quiet activity.
Stable daily routine — consistent across all 3 units
Station 1
Station 1: Keyboard letter recognition — building letter awareness.
Station 2
Station 2: Bee-Bot or ScratchJr — follow the arrows, give the robot one step at a time.
Station 3
Station 3: Sequence cards — put the picture story in order before the digital version.
Station 4
Station 4: Kodable or Bee Coding — when ready and educator directed.
Station 5
Station 5: Pattern block activity — copy the pattern, extend the pattern.
Early Finishers
Early Finishers / Break Time: Sand, paint, Starfall seasonal, or Virtual Calming Center.
Closing Routine
Cleaning and Hearts — share one safe or kind choice from today.
Typing Reminder
No speed goal. Focus: letter recognition, careful hands, name keys, arrow keys, space bar, enter, left-to-right tracking.

Device Helps or Does Not Help
Week 4 · Class 34 of 38 · Core Lesson
CSDTC
CS: Devices, inputs, outputs, people, and computers [K-2.CS.a, K-2.CS.b] Standards #1-3
Today's Agenda
Welcome Routine
Greeting, settle in, review lab norms, and connect to the unit question.
Announcements
Today’s focus is Device Helps or Does Not Help. We are working on concept practice for this unit.
Discovery Learning
Show and name the parts of a classroom device together. Students point to, touch, and repeat the name of each part before exploring independently.
Story Time
What Do You Do With a Problem? by Kobi Yamada.
Stations — Explore and Hands-On
Station 0
Station 0: Story Rug / Waiting Room — no device needed. Tracing, picture sort, or quiet activity.
Stable daily routine — consistent across all 3 units
Station 1
Station 1: Keyboard letter recognition — find the key, press it, say it.
Station 2
Station 2: Typing practice — type your name three times without looking.
Station 3
Station 3: Digital Tools Level 2 — teacher-directed device exploration.
Station 4
Station 4: What does it do? — device parts labeling activity with picture cards.
Station 5
Station 5: Classroom site — explore the approved bookmark independently.
Early Finishers
Early Finishers / Break Time: Sand, paint, Starfall seasonal, or Virtual Calming Center.
Closing Routine
Cleaning and Hearts — share one safe or kind choice from today.
Typing Reminder
No speed goal. Focus: letter recognition, careful hands, name keys, arrow keys, space bar, enter, left-to-right tracking.
W.A.L.A — We Are Learning About
We are learning how devices work, what buttons and keys do, and how simple tools follow directions.
T.I.I.B — This Is Important Because
This matters because we need tool routines before we can create with technology.
H.O.M.W.E — How Might We
How might we show how a tool listens to directions and helps us make something?
End-of-Unit PBL Choices
  • Lab Creation — draw, build, or make with classroom materials
  • Digital presentation or creation using a Clever-approved tool
  • Kodable (Grades 1–2 when educator directed)
  • Code.org (Grades 1–2 — educator directed)
  • Unplugged activity — sorting, matching, or physical building
  • Robots — Dash or school-approved device
  • Surprise me with your idea — ask your teacher first

Welcome Back to Technology Routines
Week 1 · Class 1 of 38 · Routines and Expectations
CASDTC
CAS: Safe, respectful, private, and responsible technology choices [K-2.CAS.a, K-2.CAS.b] Standards #1-3
Today's Agenda
Welcome Routine
Greeting, settle in, review lab norms, and connect to the unit question. Review routines if needed.
Announcements
Today’s focus is Welcome Back to Technology Routines. We are working on concept practice for this unit.
Discovery Learning
Read a scenario aloud and ask: "Is this information private or public?" Students vote with thumbs, then explain their reasoning to a partner.
Story Time
What Do You Do With an Idea? by Kobi Yamada.
Stations — Explore and Hands-On
Station 0
Station 0: Everyone — Typing Goat — 5 minutes.
Stable daily routine — consistent across all 3 units
Station 1
Station 1: Private vs. Public sort — physical cards, decide share or keep.
Station 2
Station 2: Trusted Adults map — draw or name who to tell when something online feels wrong.
Station 3
Station 3: Common Sense Media — teacher-directed digital citizenship activity.
Station 4
Station 4: Kodable — start or continue Smeeborg course.
Unplugged
Unplugged Station: Keyboard letter recognition activity — Fox card or arrow card sort.
Early Finishers
Early Finishers: Dance Mat Typing, Virtual Calming Center, Kodable, creativity challenges.
Closing Routine
Cleaning and Hearts — share one thing you learned or tried today.
Typing Reminder
No speed goal. Focus: letter recognition, simple words, home row awareness.
W.A.L.A — We Are Learning About
We are learning how to use digital tools safely, kindly, and with care.
T.I.I.B — This Is Important Because
This matters because our choices with technology affect ourselves, our classmates, and our shared tools.
H.O.M.W.E — How Might We
How might we show safe and kind technology habits in our classroom?
End-of-Unit PBL Choices
  • Lab Creation — draw, build, or make with classroom materials
  • Digital presentation or creation using a Clever-approved tool
  • Kodable (Grades 1–2 when educator directed)
  • Code.org (Grades 1–2 — educator directed)
  • Unplugged activity — sorting, matching, or physical building
  • Robots — Dash or school-approved device
  • Surprise me with your idea — ask your teacher first
DLCS Standards — Week 1 · Class 1 of 38
CAS: Safe, respectful, private, and responsible technology choices [K-2.CAS.a, K-2.CAS.b] Standards #1-3
DTC: Digital tools, communication, collaboration, and supported creation [K-2.DTC.a, K-2.DTC.b] Standards #1-3
This lesson targets CAS + DTC with grade appropriate language, educator directed tools, and a no tech station.
Clever apps, educator's classroom site, and school approved, monitored devices. Secure login and educator directed tools are used when they extend and reinforce learning.
Common SenseCode.orgKodableInterlandNetSmartzMakeCode
Teacher supported early reader. Use short repeated sentences, picture cues, partner talk, and short labels.
Worksheet — Welcome Back to Technology Routines
Grade 1: Draw and label. Teacher support available.
Key Vocabulary
safe—a choice that helps us stay okay
kind—using words and actions that help
private—something we do not share with everyone
Sentence Starters
How might we be safe when I ... _________________________________
I ask a trusted adult when ... _________________________________
A kind choice is ... _________________________________
Draw or Plan Here
Draw a safe technology choice.
Drawing / planning space — use the full paper packet for a larger workspace.
Role Play or Activity
Partner A shows a screen choice card. Partner B decides: safe, ask first, or stop and get help.
Tools Used Today
Digital: Typing Goat, teacher guided drawing tool, safe choice picture sort, or short classroom site activity.
Unplugged: Private or public card sort and partner talk.

Book Spotlight
What Do You Do With an Idea?
Kobi Yamada

Device Care and Class Agreements
Week 1 · Class 2 of 38 · Routines and Expectations
CASDTC
CAS: Safe, respectful, private, and responsible technology choices [K-2.CAS.a, K-2.CAS.b] Standards #1-3
Today's Agenda
Welcome Routine
Greeting, settle in, review lab norms, and connect to the unit question. Review routines if needed.
Announcements
Today’s focus is Device Care and Class Agreements. We are working on concept practice for this unit.
Discovery Learning
Read a scenario aloud and ask: "Is this information private or public?" Students vote with thumbs, then explain their reasoning to a partner.
Story Time
What Do You Do With a Problem? by Kobi Yamada.
Stations — Explore and Hands-On
Station 0
Station 0: Everyone — Typing Goat — 5 minutes.
Stable daily routine — consistent across all 3 units
Station 1
Station 1: Private vs. Public sort — physical cards, decide share or keep.
Station 2
Station 2: Trusted Adults map — draw or name who to tell when something online feels wrong.
Station 3
Station 3: Common Sense Media — teacher-directed digital citizenship activity.
Station 4
Station 4: Kodable — start or continue Smeeborg course.
Unplugged
Unplugged Station: Keyboard letter recognition activity — Fox card or arrow card sort.
Early Finishers
Early Finishers: Dance Mat Typing, Virtual Calming Center, Kodable, creativity challenges.
Closing Routine
Cleaning and Hearts — share one thing you learned or tried today.
Typing Reminder
No speed goal. Focus: letter recognition, simple words, home row awareness.
W.A.L.A — We Are Learning About
We are learning how to use digital tools safely, kindly, and with care.
T.I.I.B — This Is Important Because
This matters because our choices with technology affect ourselves, our classmates, and our shared tools.
H.O.M.W.E — How Might We
How might we show safe and kind technology habits in our classroom?
End-of-Unit PBL Choices
  • Lab Creation — draw, build, or make with classroom materials
  • Digital presentation or creation using a Clever-approved tool
  • Kodable (Grades 1–2 when educator directed)
  • Code.org (Grades 1–2 — educator directed)
  • Unplugged activity — sorting, matching, or physical building
  • Robots — Dash or school-approved device
  • Surprise me with your idea — ask your teacher first

key—a button used to type or give a command

The output is ... _________________________________

Grade 2: Write 1–2 sentences. Drawing space provided.
Key Vocabulary
algorithm—steps to solve a problem
debug—find and fix a mistake
pattern—a rule or repeated arrangement
data—information we can sort or count
Sentence Starters
My algorithm starts with ... _________________________________
The bug is ... _________________________________
I tested it by ... _________________________________
Draw or Plan Here
Draw your path, code cards, or data groups.
Drawing / planning space — use the full paper packet for a larger workspace.
Role Play or Activity
One partner reads an algorithm. One partner follows it exactly. Both find the bug and improve the steps.
Tools Used Today
Digital: CodeSpark, Code.org, Kodable basics, or digital path planning matched to the unplugged algorithm.
Unplugged: Floor grid, data sort, dust bunny clustering, paper path, bug hunt cards, or partner test.
BOOK
Book Spotlight
Ada Twist, Scientist
Andrea Beaty
Models the scientific inquiry habit of asking why and testing ideas. Used to build connection between DLCS investigation and the wider practice of curious, careful thinking.
View Book
CS Unplugged Activity
CS Unplugged: Sorting Networks
Grade level: Ages 7+ — Grade 2
What students do: Students become nodes in a network, physically sorting number cards by comparing and passing values, discovering how computers sort data in parallel.
DLCS connection: Algorithm design, parallel thinking, sequencing (CT strand)
Setup: Tape a 6-node sorting network on the floor. Pairs compare values at each node and pass cards left or right until all are sorted.
Time: 20–25 min  |  Materials: Masking tape, number cards 1–10
CS Unplugged Activity 6: Sorting Networks

CS Unplugged Activity
CS Unplugged: Binary Numbers
Grade level: Ages 6+ — Grade 2
What students do: Students use 5 dot-cards to represent numbers 0–31, discovering how computers store all information as on/off signals.
DLCS connection: How computers represent data, systems (CS strand)
Setup: Give each student 5 dot-cards. Call out numbers; flip cards up or down. Connect to pixels, files, and memory.
Time: 15–20 min  |  Materials: Printed dot-cards (1, 2, 4, 8, 16 dots)

Station 0
Station 0: Typing Club (Clever) or Kodable Typing — 10 minutes. Build toward 15 WPM.
Stable daily routine — consistent across all 3 units
Station 1
Station 1: MediaSmarts or Common Sense Media — teacher-assigned lesson on source credibility.
Station 2
Station 2: Partner discussion — Is this true? Evidence check with a curated article set.
Station 3
Station 3: Unplugged — Digital dilemma cards: what would you do? Record your reasoning.
Station 4
Station 4: Code.org — CS Fundamentals course (teacher assigned current level).
Early Finishers
Early Finishers: Code.org challenges, Virtual Calming Center, or Typing Club / Kodable Typing (Clever).
Closing Routine
Cleaning and Hearts — share one thing you created or discovered.
Typing Reminder
Goal: 15 words per minute by end of third grade.
W.A.L.A — We Are Learning About
We are learning how digital choices, privacy, communication, and digital footprints affect people.
T.I.I.B — This Is Important Because
This matters because responsible digital citizens think before they click, share, search, or post.
H.O.M.W.E — How Might We
How might we shape our digital choices so they are safe, respectful, and helpful?
End-of-Unit PBL Choices
  • Lab Creation — diagram, model, or physical prototype
  • Digital presentation or creation (Canva Education, Google Slides)
  • Kodable Creator or Kodable game design
  • Code.org final project of your choice under Creativity
  • Microsoft MakeCode and Micro:bit project
  • Google Docs or Sheets research or data project
  • Surprise me with your idea — ask your teacher first

CS Unplugged Activity
CS Unplugged: Information Hiding — Caesar Cipher
Grade level: Ages 8+ — Grade 3
What students do: Students encode and decode messages using a Caesar cipher, connecting encryption to why privacy protection matters online.
DLCS connection: Privacy, why personal information needs protection (CAS strand)
Setup: Provide alphabet shift wheels. Encode a short message; swap; decode. Discuss: what if the key is discovered?

Worksheet — Algorithms With Precision
Grade 3: Write in complete sentences. Vocabulary box for support.
Key Vocabulary
algorithm—ordered steps to solve a problem
debug—find and fix an error
loop—a repeat command
data—information used by a program or person
program—instructions a computer follows
Sentence Starters
My algorithm solves ... _________________________________
I debugged by ... _________________________________
I improved the project by ... _________________________________
Draw or Plan Here
Sketch or write your algorithm, test, bug, and fix.
Drawing / planning space — use the full paper packet for a larger workspace.
Role Play or Activity
One partner is the programmer. One partner is the debugger. Test the algorithm, name the bug, and suggest one improvement.
Tools Used Today
Digital: Kodable Basics, Kodable Creator, Kodable Typing, Code.org, or Google Slides planning.
Unplugged: Paper algorithm, flowchart, data cards, test case table, peer feedback, or debugging log.
BOOK
Book Spotlight
Mistakes That Worked
Charlotte Foltz Jones
Celebrates accidental discoveries that changed history. Reframes error as productive and connects to debugging, persistence, and the unpredictable path of innovation.
View Book
CS Unplugged Activity
CS Unplugged: Programming Languages — Precise Instructions
Grade level: Ages 7+ — Grade 3
What students do: Students write step-by-step instructions for drawing a shape. A partner follows them exactly — discovering that ambiguity causes bugs and precision is essential.
DLCS connection: Algorithm design, debugging, clear language (CT strand)
Setup: Pairs sit back-to-back. One draws a shape; the other writes instructions. A third follows only the written instructions. Compare and debug.
Time: 25–30 min  |  Materials: Paper, pencil, ruler

CS Unplugged Activity
CS Unplugged: Network Communication — Passing Packets
Grade level: Ages 7+ — Grade 3
What students do: Students simulate a network by passing index cards (packets) across the classroom through multiple routers, experiencing routing, delay, and packet loss.
DLCS connection: How networks communicate, data packets, systems (CS strand)
Setup: Students act as routers in a star or mesh. Write a message across 3 cards. Route them; remove one mid-transmission. How does the receiver know?
Time: 20–25 min  |  Materials: Index cards, network diagram on board

CTDTC
CT: Algorithms, abstraction, data, programming, debugging, modeling, and iteration [3-5.CT.a, 3-5.CT.b, 3-5.CT.d] Standa...
Today's Agenda
Welcome Routine
Greeting, settle in, review lab norms, and connect to the unit question. Review routines if needed.
Announcements
Today’s focus is Designing Algorithms for Users. We are working on concept practice for this unit.
Discovery Learning
Show a program with a hidden bug. Students read the code, predict the output, run it mentally, then propose a fix with precise language.
Story Time
The Dot by Peter H. Reynolds.
Stations — Explore and Hands-On
Station 0
Station 0: Typing Club (Clever) — 10 minutes. Build toward 20 WPM.
Station 1
Station 1: Work on your Resume and Jobs project (Canva Education or Google Slides).
Station 2
Station 2: Code.org — assigned project (CS Fundamentals Accelerated or course level).
Station 3
Station 3: Debugging challenge — find and fix the error in the printed algorithm.
Genius Bar
Let your teacher know when your resume project is ready so we can print or share it.
Early Finishers
Early Finishers: Typing Club / Kodable Typing, Virtual Calming Center, or Jobs / Resume / Business Cards project.
Closing Routine
Cleaning and Hearts — share one challenge you worked through today.
Typing Reminder
Goal: 20 words per minute by end of fourth grade.
W.A.L.A — We Are Learning About
We are learning how to write precise algorithms and trace each step to predict what a program will do before running it.
T.I.I.B — This Is Important Because
This matters because strong creators plan, test, improve, and explain their decisions.
H.O.M.W.E — How Might We
How might we build and improve a project that uses logic, creativity, and feedback?

loop—a structure that repeats steps a set number of times or until a condition is met
data—collected information that can be sorted, displayed, and used to support a conclusion
program—instructions written for a computer
Sentence Starters
My algorithm solves ... by first ... then ... using a loop or conditional when ... _________________________________
I debugged by finding ... , changing ... , and testing that the fix worked because ... _________________________________
I improved the project by changing ... which made it better because ... _________________________________
Draw or Plan Here
Sketch or write your algorithm, test, bug, and fix.
Drawing / planning space — use the full paper packet for a larger workspace.
Role Play or Activity
One partner is the programmer. One partner is the debugger. Test the algorithm, name the bug, and suggest one improvement.
Tools Used Today
Digital: Kodable Creator, Code.org, Microsoft MakeCode, Google Sheets data table, or Dash robot task.
Unplugged: Flowchart cards, loop cards, variable cards, data table cards, peer review checklist, or project role cards.

CS Unplugged Activity
CS Unplugged: Searching Algorithms
Grade level: Ages 9+ — Grade 4
What students do: Students compare linear search to binary search using sealed envelopes, discovering that binary search is dramatically more efficient on sorted data.
DLCS connection: Algorithm efficiency, data structures, computational thinking (CT strand)
Setup: Prepare 20 envelopes numbered 1–20 with one prize. Linear: open from left. Binary: open middle, decide which half. Count and compare.
Time: 25–30 min  |  Materials: 20 numbered envelopes, one with a prize card

12 classes · We are learning how hardware, software, circuits, robots, and tools work as systems....
W.A.L.A T.I.I.B H.O.M.W.E
W.A.L.A — We Are Learning About
We are learning how hardware, software, circuits, robots, and tools work as systems.
T.I.I.B — This Is Important Because
This matters because systems thinking helps us troubleshoot and make informed choices.
H.O.M.W.E — How Might We
How might we design a system, test how it works, and explain why our tool choice fits the task?
End-of-Unit PBL Choices
  • Lab Creation — diagram, model, or physical prototype
  • Digital presentation or creation (Canva Education, Google Slides)
  • Kodable Creator or Kodable game design
  • Code.org final project of your choice under Creativity
  • Microsoft MakeCode and Micro:bit project
  • Google Docs or Sheets research or data project
  • Surprise me with your idea — ask your teacher first

Hardware, Software, and Data
Week 1 · Class 27 of 38 · Core Lesson
CSDTC
CS: Hardware, software, networks, systems, troubleshooting, and tool choice [3-5.CS.a, 3-5.CS.b] Standards #1-4
Today's Agenda
Welcome Routine
Greeting, settle in, review lab norms, and connect to the unit question. Review routines if needed.
Announcements
Today’s focus is Hardware, Software, and Data. We are working on concept practice for this unit.
Discovery Learning
Open the back of an old computer or a labeled diagram. Students match each component to its function before the independent station work.
Story Time
How to Code a Sandcastle by Josh Funk.
Stations — Explore and Hands-On
Station 0
Group Station: Think Station — teacher led on projector or chart paper. Review the concept together.
Station 1
Station 1: Digital Tool Station — Dash robot, MakeCode, Canva, or Google Sites exploration.
Station 2
Station 2: Systems diagram — draw the hardware and software components of one school tool.
Station 3
Station 3: Unplugged — troubleshooting scenarios: what broke, what would you check first?
Early Finishers
Typing Club or Kodable Typing (Clever), Virtual Calming Center, creativity, or Jobs / Resume / Business Cards project.
Closing Routine
Cleaning and Hearts — share one challenge you worked through today.
Typing Reminder
Goal: 20 words per minute by end of fourth grade.

  • Digital presentation or creation (Canva Education, Google Slides)
  • Kodable Creator or Kodable game design
  • Code.org final project of your choice under Creativity
  • Microsoft MakeCode and Micro:bit project
  • Google Docs or Sheets research or data project

DLCS Standards — Week 1 · Class 27 of 38
CS: Hardware, software, networks, systems, troubleshooting, and tool choice [3-5.CS.a, 3-5.CS.b] Standards #1-4
DTC: Choose and use approved tools for purpose, communication, and creation [3-5.DTC.a, 3-5.DTC.b] Standards #1-3
This lesson targets CS + DTC with grade appropriate language, educator directed tools, and a no tech station.
Clever apps, educator's classroom site, and school approved, monitored devices. Secure login and educator directed tools are used when they extend and reinforce learning.
Common SenseCode.orgKodableInterlandNetSmartzMakeCode
Upper elementary reader. Use multi step planning, peer feedback, user needs, and project reflection.
Worksheet — Hardware, Software, and Data
Grade 4: Write a short paragraph. Use evidence from stations.
Key Vocabulary
system—connected parts that work together
input—data or action a system receives
output—the result a system produces
network—devices or systems connected to share information
tool choice—selecting a tool based on purpose and user needs
Sentence Starters
This system works by ... _________________________________
The best tool for this task is ... because ... _________________________________
This design supports users by ... _________________________________
Draw or Plan Here
Sketch the system, tool choice, input, process, and output.
Drawing / planning space — use the full paper packet for a larger workspace.
Role Play or Activity
Team members role play hardware, software, input, output, user, and troubleshooter to explain a system.
Tools Used Today
Digital: Dash robot, Microsoft MakeCode, Canva, Google Slides, Google Docs, or systems explanation.
Unplugged: Circuit cards, system diagram, network pathway role play, troubleshooting evidence cards, or accessibility redesign cards.
BOOK
Book Spotlight
How to Code a Sandcastle
Josh Funk
Demonstrates algorithmic thinking with concrete, physical steps. Grounds abstract coding ideas in real-world sequencing and debugging experiences.
View Book
CS Unplugged Activity
CS Unplugged: Image Representation — Pixel Art
Grade level: Ages 8+ — Grade 4
What students do: Students encode a pixel image as run-length encoding, then exchange codes and decode a peer's image, connecting to how digital images are stored.
DLCS connection: How computers represent data, input/output, digital tools (CS + DTC)
Setup: On 10×10 grid paper, shade a simple image. Write run-length encoding. Exchange codes with a partner and decode theirs.
Time: 30 min  |  Materials: Grid paper, pencils
CS Unplugged Activity 2: Image Representation

Grade 5 · Unit 1 of 3 · CAS + DTC
Digital Life, Safety, and Impact
14 classes · We are learning how digital footprints, privacy, media choices, data, and technology impac...
W.A.L.A T.I.I.B H.O.M.W.E
W.A.L.A — We Are Learning About
We are learning how digital footprints, privacy, media choices, data, and technology impacts connect to leadership and responsibility.
T.I.I.B — This Is Important Because
This matters because older elementary learners need habits for safe, ethical, and thoughtful digital participation.
H.O.M.W.E — How Might We
How might we create digital choices that reflect the kind of community member we want to be?
End-of-Unit PBL Choices
  • Lab Creation — diagram, model, or physical prototype
  • Digital presentation or creation (Canva Education, Google Slides)
  • Kodable Creator or Kodable game design
  • Code.org final project of your choice under Creativity
  • Microsoft MakeCode and Micro:bit project
  • Google Docs or Sheets research or data project
  • Surprise me with your idea — ask your teacher first

Digital Leadership and Agency
Week 1 · Class 1 of 38 · Routines and Expectations
CASDTC
CAS: Safe, respectful, private, and responsible technology choices [3-5.CAS.a, 3-5.CAS.b] Standards #1-3
Today's Agenda
Welcome Routine
Greeting, settle in, review lab norms, and connect to the unit question. Review routines if needed.
Announcements
Today’s focus is Digital Leadership and Agency. We are working on concept practice for this unit.
Discovery Learning
Present an AI-generated image and a real photograph on the projector. Students identify three differences and discuss how they would verify which is real.
Story Time
Grace Hopper: Queen of Computer Code by Laurie Wallmark.
Stations — Explore and Hands-On
Station 0
Group Station: Think Station — teacher led on projector or chart paper. Review, discuss, take notes.
Station 1
Station 1: Digital Tool Station — Interland or PBS NOVA Cybersecurity Lab (teacher assigned).
Station 2
Station 2: Practice Station — partner talk, planning mat, cards, or classroom materials.
Station 3
Station 3: Unplugged — media message cards, privacy analysis, or ethical scenario cards.
Early Finishers
Typing Club (Clever), Virtual Calming Center, creativity challenges, or Jobs / Resume / Business Cards project.
Closing Routine
Cleaning and Hearts — share one idea or connection from today's work.
Typing Reminder
Goal: 25 words per minute by end of fifth grade.
W.A.L.A — We Are Learning About
We are learning how digital footprints, privacy, media choices, data, and technology impacts connect to leadership and responsibility.
T.I.I.B — This Is Important Because
This matters because older elementary learners need habits for safe, ethical, and thoughtful digital participation.
H.O.M.W.E — How Might We
How might we create digital choices that reflect the kind of community member we want to be?
End-of-Unit PBL Choices
  • Lab Creation — diagram, model, or physical prototype
  • Digital presentation or creation (Canva Education, Google Slides)
  • Kodable Creator or Kodable game design
  • Code.org final project of your choice under Creativity
  • Microsoft MakeCode and Micro:bit project
  • Google Docs or Sheets research or data project
  • Surprise me with your idea — ask your teacher first
DLCS Standards — Week 1 · Class 1 of 38
CAS: Safe, respectful, private, and responsible technology choices [3-5.CAS.a, 3-5.CAS.b] Standards #1-3
DTC: Digital tools, communication, collaboration, and supported creation [3-5.DTC.a, 3-5.DTC.b] Standards #1-3
This lesson targets CAS + DTC with grade appropriate language, educator directed tools, and a no tech station.
Clever apps, educator's classroom site, and school approved, monitored devices. Secure login and educator directed tools are used when they extend and reinforce learning.
Common SenseCode.orgKodableInterlandNetSmartzMakeCode
Upper elementary reader. Use longer reasoning prompts, evaluation criteria, and human centered reflection.
Worksheet — Digital Leadership and Agency
Grade 5: Write an extended response. Cite tools and sources used.
Key Vocabulary
privacy—protecting information and respecting consent
digital footprint—the lasting record shaped by digital choices
source—the origin of information used to judge reliability
credit—acknowledging original work or sources
impact—the larger effect of technology on people or communities
Sentence Starters
The responsible choice is ... and I know this because the evidence shows ... _________________________________
This affects people differently depending on ... and that matters because ... _________________________________
To protect privacy in this situation, I would ... which addresses the risk of ... _________________________________
Draw or Plan Here
Sketch the situation and mark the responsible choice.
Drawing / planning space — use the full paper packet for a larger workspace.
Role Play or Activity
One partner presents a digital situation. Partners discuss privacy, impact, and a responsible next step.
Tools Used Today
Digital: Google Slides, Canva, Google Docs, or source verification organizer with privacy and impact reflection.
Unplugged: Media message cards, privacy and consent cards, source verification mat, or impact map.
BOOK
Book Spotlight
Grace Hopper: Queen of Computer Code
Laurie Wallmark
Introduces a real computing pioneer and her legacy. Anchors discussion about persistence, precision, and the people who built the systems we use today.
View Book

Accessibility and Human Centered Design
Week 4 · Class 8 of 38 · Core Lesson
CASDTC
CAS: Safe, respectful, private, and responsible technology choices [3-5.CAS.a, 3-5.CAS.b] Standards #1-3
Today's Agenda
Welcome Routine
Greeting, settle in, review lab norms, and connect to the unit question.
Announcements
Today’s focus is Accessibility and Human Centered Design. We are working on concept practice for this unit.
Discovery Learning
Present an AI-generated image and a real photograph on the projector. Students identify three differences and discuss how they would verify which is real.
Story Time
Rosie Revere, Engineer by Andrea Beaty.
Stations — Explore and Hands-On
Station 0
Group Station: Think Station — teacher led on projector or chart paper. Review, discuss, take notes.
Station 1
Station 1: Digital Tool Station — Interland or PBS NOVA Cybersecurity Lab (teacher assigned).
Station 2
Station 2: Practice Station — partner talk, planning mat, cards, or classroom materials.
Station 3
Station 3: Unplugged — media message cards, privacy analysis, or ethical scenario cards.
Early Finishers
Typing Club (Clever), Virtual Calming Center, creativity challenges, or Jobs / Resume / Business Cards project.
Closing Routine
Cleaning and Hearts — share one idea or connection from today's work.
Typing Reminder
Goal: 25 words per minute by end of fifth grade.
W.A.L.A — We Are Learning About
We are learning how digital footprints, privacy, media choices, data, and technology impacts connect to leadership and responsibility.
T.I.I.B — This Is Important Because
This matters because older elementary learners need habits for safe, ethical, and thoughtful digital participation.
H.O.M.W.E — How Might We
How might we create digital choices that reflect the kind of community member we want to be?
End-of-Unit PBL Choices
  • Lab Creation — diagram, model, or physical prototype
  • Digital presentation or creation (Canva Education, Google Slides)
  • Kodable Creator or Kodable game design
  • Code.org final project of your choice under Creativity
  • Microsoft MakeCode and Micro:bit project
  • Google Docs or Sheets research or data project
  • Surprise me with your idea — ask your teacher first
DLCS Standards — Week 4 · Class 8 of 38
CAS: Safe, respectful, private, and responsible technology choices [3-5.CAS.a, 3-5.CAS.b] Standards #1-3
DTC: Digital tools, communication, collaboration, and supported creation [3-5.DTC.a, 3-5.DTC.b] Standards #1-3
This lesson targets CAS + DTC with grade appropriate language, educator directed tools, and a no tech station.
Clever apps, educator's classroom site, and school approved, monitored devices. Secure login and educator directed tools are used when they extend and reinforce learning.
Common SenseCode.orgKodableInterlandNetSmartzMakeCode
Upper elementary reader. Use longer reasoning prompts, evaluation criteria, and human centered reflection.
Worksheet — Accessibility and Human Centered Design
Grade 5: Write an extended response. Cite tools and sources used.
Key Vocabulary
privacy—protecting information and respecting consent
digital footprint—the lasting record shaped by digital choices
source—the origin of information used to judge reliability
credit—acknowledging original work or sources
impact—the larger effect of technology on people or communities
Sentence Starters
The responsible choice is ... and I know this because the evidence shows ... _________________________________
This affects people differently depending on ... and that matters because ... _________________________________
To protect privacy in this situation, I would ... which addresses the risk of ... _________________________________
Draw or Plan Here
Sketch the situation and mark the responsible choice.
Drawing / planning space — use the full paper packet for a larger workspace.
Role Play or Activity
One partner presents a digital situation. Partners discuss privacy, impact, and a responsible next step.
Tools Used Today
Digital: Google Slides, Canva, Google Docs, or source verification organizer with privacy and impact reflection.
Unplugged: Media message cards, privacy and consent cards, source verification mat, or impact map.
BOOK
Book Spotlight
Rosie Revere, Engineer
Andrea Beaty
Models the iterative design cycle through Rosie's cheerful failures. Used to introduce testing, improvement, and the idea that a good flop is a step forward.

Common SenseCode.orgKodableInterlandNetSmartzMakeCode

Worksheet — Algorithm Design for a Purpose
Grade 5: Write an extended response. Cite tools and sources used.
Key Vocabulary
algorithm—a precise set of instructions for a process
debug—use evidence to locate and fix errors
loop—a structure that repeats instructions efficiently
data—information stored, changed, compared, or used
program—a designed set of instructions a computer runs
Sentence Starters
My algorithm solves ... by decomposing the problem into ... and using ... to handle each case ... _________________________________
I debugged by isolating ... , testing the hypothesis that ... , and confirming the fix worked because ... _________________________________
I improved the project by changing ... , which affected the output by ... , as shown by ... _________________________________
Draw or Plan Here
Sketch or write your algorithm, test, bug, and fix.
Drawing / planning space — use the full paper packet for a larger workspace.
Role Play or Activity
One partner is the programmer. One partner is the debugger. Test the algorithm, name the bug, and suggest one improvement.
Tools Used Today
Digital: Kodable Creator, Code.org, Microsoft MakeCode, Micro Bit, Google Sheets, Docs planning, or Canva project planning.
Unplugged: Algorithm planning mat for mapping ordered steps before coding; function cards for grouping repeated actions into reusable routines; data model cards for sorting information into categories, attributes, and examples; debugging log for naming what did not work and documenting a tested fix; peer feedback protocol for giving kind, specific, and useful suggestions; or user need cards for connecting a design choice to the needs of an intended audience.
BOOK
Book Spotlight
What Do You Do With an Idea?
Kobi Yamada
Explores how ideas grow when we protect and nurture them. Anchors discussion about creative thinking, persistence, and sharing work with an audience.
View Book
CS Unplugged Activity
CS Unplugged: Finite State Automata — Treasure Hunt
Grade level: Ages 7+ — richly applicable at Grade 5
What students do: Students navigate a treasure hunt using a state-machine diagram. They discover that programs are state machines — output depends on both current state and current input.
DLCS connection: Algorithms, conditionals, how programs respond to input (CT strand)
Setup: Post a 6-node state diagram. Students navigate by reading input clue cards and following transitions. Discuss: which conditional governs each move?
Time: 30–35 min  |  Materials: State diagram poster, clue cards, 6 labeled classroom locations
CS Unplugged Activity 14: Finite State Automata

Station 0: Typing Club (Clever) — 10 minutes. Build toward 25 WPM with accuracy.
Station 1
Station 1: Clever — Code.org assigned project (CS Fundamentals or Accelerated CS).
Station 2
Station 2: Kodable — Python Game Creator or Kodable Creator game design.
Station 3
Station 3: Code.org — open-ended Creativity project of your choice.
Genius Bar
When you finish your Unit project, let the teacher or a Genius on Duty know so we can print your QR code.
Early Finishers
Early Finishers: Typing Club / Kodable Typing, Virtual Calming Center, creativity, or Jobs / Resume / Business Cards project.
Closing Routine
Cleaning and Hearts — share one idea or connection from today's work.
Typing Reminder
Goal: 25 words per minute by end of fifth grade.
W.A.L.A — We Are Learning About
We are learning how to trace a program for bugs, name the error precisely, test a fix, and document what changed and why.
T.I.I.B — This Is Important Because
This matters because computational thinking helps us solve bigger problems with precision and creativity.
H.O.M.W.E — How Might We
How might we design and improve a digital solution that helps others?
End-of-Unit PBL Choices
  • Lab Creation — diagram, model, or physical prototype
  • Digital presentation or creation (Canva Education, Google Slides)
  • Kodable Creator or Kodable game design
  • Code.org final project of your choice under Creativity
  • Microsoft MakeCode and Micro:bit project
  • Google Docs or Sheets research or data project
  • Surprise me with your idea — ask your teacher first
DLCS Standards — Week 3 · Class 20 of 38
CT: Algorithms, abstraction, data, programming, debugging, modeling, and iteration [3-5.CT.a, 3-5.CT.b, 3-5.CT.d] Standards #1-5
DTC: Use approved tools to create, communicate, revise, and explain thinking [3-5.DTC.a, 3-5.DTC.b] Standards #1-3

Common SenseCode.orgKodableInterlandNetSmartzMakeCode
Upper elementary reader. Use longer reasoning prompts, evaluation criteria, and human centered reflection.
Worksheet — Simulation and Testing
Grade 5: Write an extended response. Cite tools and sources used.
Key Vocabulary
algorithm—a precise set of instructions for a process
debug—use evidence to locate and fix errors
loop—a structure that repeats instructions efficiently
data—information stored, changed, compared, or used
program—a designed set of instructions a computer runs
Sentence Starters
My algorithm solves ... by decomposing the problem into ... and using ... to handle each case ... _________________________________
I debugged by isolating ... , testing the hypothesis that ... , and confirming the fix worked because ... _________________________________
I improved the project by changing ... , which affected the output by ... , as shown by ... _________________________________
Draw or Plan Here
Sketch or write your algorithm, test, bug, and fix.
Drawing / planning space — use the full paper packet for a larger workspace.
Role Play or Activity
One partner is the programmer. One partner is the debugger. Test the algorithm, name the bug, and suggest one improvement.
Tools Used Today
Digital: Kodable Creator, Code.org, Microsoft MakeCode, Micro Bit, Google Sheets, Docs planning, or Canva project planning.
Unplugged: Algorithm planning mat for mapping ordered steps before coding; function cards for grouping repeated actions into reusable routines; data model cards for sorting information into categories, attributes, and examples; debugging log for naming what did not work and documenting a tested fix; peer feedback protocol for giving kind, specific, and useful suggestions; or user need cards for connecting a design choice to the needs of an intended audience.
BOOK
Book Spotlight
The Most Magnificent Thing
Ashley Spires
Follows a maker through frustration and breakthrough. Anchors lessons on persistence, debugging, and the emotional side of the creative process.
View Book
CS Unplugged Activity
CS Unplugged: Finite State Automata — Treasure Hunt
Grade level: Ages 7+ — richly applicable at Grade 5
What students do: Students navigate a treasure hunt using a state-machine diagram. They discover that programs are state machines — output depends on both current state and current input.
DLCS connection: Algorithms, conditionals, how programs respond to input (CT strand)
Setup: Post a 6-node state diagram. Students navigate by reading input clue cards and following transitions. Discuss: which conditional governs each move?
Time: 30–35 min  |  Materials: State diagram poster, clue cards, 6 labeled classroom locations
CS Unplugged Activity 14: Finite State Automata

What students do: Students navigate a treasure hunt using a state-machine diagram. They discover that programs are state machines — output depends on both current state and current input.
DLCS connection: Algorithms, conditionals, how programs respond to input (CT strand)
Setup: Post a 6-node state diagram. Students navigate by reading input clue cards and following transitions. Discuss: which conditional governs each move?
Time: 30–35 min  |  Materials: State diagram poster, clue cards, 6 labeled classroom locations

Worksheet — Project Share and Reflect
Grade 5: Write an extended response. Cite tools and sources used.
Key Vocabulary
algorithm—a precise set of instructions for a process
debug—use evidence to locate and fix errors
loop—a structure that repeats instructions efficiently
data—information stored, changed, compared, or used
program—a designed set of instructions a computer runs
Sentence Starters
My algorithm solves ... by decomposing the problem into ... and using ... to handle each case ... _________________________________
I debugged by isolating ... , testing the hypothesis that ... , and confirming the fix worked because ... _________________________________
I improved the project by changing ... , which affected the output by ... , as shown by ... _________________________________
Draw or Plan Here
Sketch or write your algorithm, test, bug, and fix.
Drawing / planning space — use the full paper packet for a larger workspace.
Role Play or Activity
One partner is the programmer. One partner is the debugger. Test the algorithm, name the bug, and suggest one improvement.
Tools Used Today
Digital: Kodable Creator, Code.org, Microsoft MakeCode, Micro Bit, Google Sheets, Docs planning, or Canva project planning.
Unplugged: Algorithm planning mat for mapping ordered steps before coding; function cards for grouping repeated actions into reusable routines; data model cards for sorting information into categories, attributes, and examples; debugging log for naming what did not work and documenting a tested fix; peer feedback protocol for giving kind, specific, and useful suggestions; or user need cards for connecting a design choice to the needs of an intended audience.

Worksheet — Computing Systems Around Us
Grade 5: Write an extended response. Cite tools and sources used.
Key Vocabulary
system—interdependent components that work together to perform a function — a change to one part affects the whole
input—the data, signal, or command that enters a system and triggers processing
output—the result a system produces after processing input, which may itself become input to another system
network—connected systems that move information between places
tool choice—evaluating which tool best fits purpose, privacy, and access
Sentence Starters
This system works by ... and when one component fails, the effect on the whole system is ... _________________________________
The best tool for this task is ... because it addresses the requirements of ... while considering accessibility and privacy by ... _________________________________
This design supports users by ... and I know it is inclusive because ... _________________________________
Draw or Plan Here
Sketch the system, tool choice, input, process, and output.
Drawing / planning space — use the full paper packet for a larger workspace.
Role Play or Activity
Team members role play hardware, software, input, output, user, and troubleshooter to explain a system.
Tools Used Today
Digital: Micro Bit, Microsoft MakeCode, Dash robot, Canva, Google Slides, Docs, Sheets, or systems design artifact.
Unplugged: System model cards, network pathway map, troubleshooting protocol, accessibility audit, or privacy and tool choice comparison.
BOOK
Book Spotlight
The Most Magnificent Thing
Ashley Spires
Follows a maker through frustration and breakthrough. Anchors lessons on persistence, debugging, and the emotional side of the creative process.
View Book
CS Unplugged Activity
CS Unplugged: Network Protocols — Four-Point Protocol
Grade level: Ages 9+ — Grade 5
What students do: Students simulate reliable transmission: sender sends packets one at a time; receiver acknowledges each. The facilitator removes one — students discover how the internet ensures complete, ordered delivery.
DLCS connection: Networks, cybersecurity, systems reliability and protocol design (CS strand)
Setup: Pairs: sender writes a 5-sentence message on 5 cards. Receiver thumbs-up each ACK. Facilitator secretly removes one. What does the sender do?
Time: 25–30 min  |  Materials: Index cards, facilitator to simulate packet loss
CS Unplugged Activity 12 (advanced): Network Protocols

View Book
CS Unplugged Activity
CS Unplugged: Network Protocols — Four-Point Protocol
Grade level: Ages 9+ — Grade 5
What students do: Students simulate reliable transmission: sender sends packets one at a time; receiver acknowledges each. The facilitator removes one — students discover how the internet ensures complete, ordered delivery.
DLCS connection: Networks, cybersecurity, systems reliability and protocol design (CS strand)
Setup: Pairs: sender writes a 5-sentence message on 5 cards. Receiver thumbs-up each ACK. Facilitator secretly removes one. What does the sender do?
Time: 25–30 min  |  Materials: Index cards, facilitator to simulate packet loss
CS Unplugged Activity 12 (advanced): Network Protocols

Accessibility and Assistive Technologies
Week 3 · Class 31 of 38 · Core Lesson
CSDTC
CS: Hardware, software, networks, systems, troubleshooting, and tool choice [3-5.CS.a, 3-5.CS.b] Standards #1-4
Today's Agenda
Welcome Routine
Greeting, settle in, review lab norms, and connect to the unit question.
Announcements
Today’s focus is Accessibility and Assistive Technologies. We are working on concept practice for this unit.
Discovery Learning
Diagram a school network live on the board with student input. Students add devices, label connections, and identify where a failure would break the system.
Story Time
Grace Hopper: Queen of Computer Code by Laurie Wallmark.
Stations — Explore and Hands-On
Station 0
Group Station: Think Station — teacher led on projector or chart paper. Review and connect to prior learning.
Station 1
Station 1: Digital Tool Station — Micro:bit, MakeCode, Dash robot, or Canva portfolio.
Station 2
Station 2: Systems explainer — write or sketch how one technology system works end to end.
Station 3
Station 3: Unplugged — binary, logic, or encryption puzzle activity.
Early Finishers
Typing Club (Clever), Virtual Calming Center, creativity challenges, or Jobs / Resume / Business Cards project.
Closing Routine
Cleaning and Hearts — share one idea or connection from today's work.
Typing Reminder
Goal: 25 words per minute by end of fifth grade.
W.A.L.A — We Are Learning About
We are learning how computing systems, networks, devices, accessibility, and tools work together.
T.I.I.B — This Is Important Because
This matters because tool choices and system design reflect values — who is included, who is excluded, and who bears the consequences of design decisions.
H.O.M.W.E — How Might We
How might we evaluate systems and tools so our choices are useful, safe, and inclusive?
End-of-Unit PBL Choices
  • Lab Creation — diagram, model, or physical prototype
  • Digital presentation or creation (Canva Education, Google Slides)
  • Kodable Creator or Kodable game design
  • Code.org final project of your choice under Creativity
  • Microsoft MakeCode and Micro:bit project
  • Google Docs or Sheets research or data project
  • Surprise me with your idea — ask your teacher first
DLCS Standards — Week 3 · Class 31 of 38
CS: Hardware, software, networks, systems, troubleshooting, and tool choice [3-5.CS.a, 3-5.CS.b] Standards #1-4
DTC: Choose and use approved tools for purpose, communication, and creation [3-5.DTC.a, 3-5.DTC.b] Standards #1-3

Common SenseCode.orgKodableInterlandNetSmartzMakeCode
Upper elementary reader. Use longer reasoning prompts, evaluation criteria, and human centered reflection.
Worksheet — Accessibility and Assistive Technologies
Grade 5: Write an extended response. Cite tools and sources used.
Key Vocabulary
system—interdependent components that work together to perform a function — a change to one part affects the whole
input—the data, signal, or command that enters a system and triggers processing
output—the result a system produces after processing input, which may itself become input to another system
network—connected systems that move information between places
tool choice—evaluating which tool best fits purpose, privacy, and access
Sentence Starters
This system works by ... and when one component fails, the effect on the whole system is ... _________________________________
The best tool for this task is ... because it addresses the requirements of ... while considering accessibility and privacy by ... _________________________________
This design supports users by ... and I know it is inclusive because ... _________________________________
Draw or Plan Here
Sketch the system, tool choice, input, process, and output.
Drawing / planning space — use the full paper packet for a larger workspace.
Role Play or Activity
Team members role play hardware, software, input, output, user, and troubleshooter to explain a system.
Tools Used Today
Digital: Micro Bit, Microsoft MakeCode, Dash robot, Canva, Google Slides, Docs, Sheets, or systems design artifact.
Unplugged: System model cards, network pathway map, troubleshooting protocol, accessibility audit, or privacy and tool choice comparison.

CS Unplugged: Network Protocols — Four-Point Protocol
Grade level: Ages 9+ — Grade 5
What students do: Students simulate reliable transmission: sender sends packets one at a time; receiver acknowledges each. The facilitator removes one — students discover how the internet ensures complete, ordered delivery.
DLCS connection: Networks, cybersecurity, systems reliability and protocol design (CS strand)
Setup: Pairs: sender writes a 5-sentence message on 5 cards. Receiver thumbs-up each ACK. Facilitator secretly removes one. What does the sender do?
Time: 25–30 min  |  Materials: Index cards, facilitator to simulate packet loss

Today's Agenda
Welcome Routine
Greeting, settle in, review lab norms, and connect to the unit question.
Announcements
Today’s focus is Systems Project Build. We are working on project building for this unit.
Discovery Learning
Diagram a school network live on the board with student input. Students add devices, label connections, and identify where a failure would break the system.
Story Time
What Do You Do With a Problem? by Kobi Yamada.
Stations — Explore and Hands-On
Station 0
Group Station: Think Station — teacher led on projector or chart paper. Review and connect to prior learning.
Station 1
Station 1: Digital Tool Station — Micro:bit, MakeCode, Dash robot, or Canva portfolio.
Station 2
Station 2: Systems explainer — write or sketch how one technology system works end to end.
Station 3
Station 3: Unplugged — binary, logic, or encryption puzzle activity.
Early Finishers
Typing Club (Clever), Virtual Calming Center, creativity challenges, or Jobs / Resume / Business Cards project.
Closing Routine
Cleaning and Hearts — share one idea or connection from today's work.
Typing Reminder
Goal: 25 words per minute by end of fifth grade.
W.A.L.A — We Are Learning About
We are learning how computing systems, networks, devices, accessibility, and tools work together.
T.I.I.B — This Is Important Because
This matters because tool choices and system design reflect values — who is included, who is excluded, and who bears the consequences of design decisions.
H.O.M.W.E — How Might We
How might we evaluate systems and tools so our choices are useful, safe, and inclusive?
End-of-Unit PBL Choices
  • Lab Creation — diagram, model, or physical prototype
  • Digital presentation or creation (Canva Education, Google Slides)
  • Kodable Creator or Kodable game design
  • Code.org final project of your choice under Creativity
  • Microsoft MakeCode and Micro:bit project
  • Google Docs or Sheets research or data project
  • Surprise me with your idea — ask your teacher first

Worksheet — Systems Project Build
Grade 5: Write an extended response. Cite tools and sources used.
Key Vocabulary
system—interdependent components that work together to perform a function — a change to one part affects the whole
input—the data, signal, or command that enters a system and triggers processing
output—the result a system produces after processing input, which may itself become input to another system
network—connected systems that move information between places
tool choice—evaluating which tool best fits purpose, privacy, and access
Sentence Starters
This system works by ... and when one component fails, the effect on the whole system is ... _________________________________
The best tool for this task is ... because it addresses the requirements of ... while considering accessibility and privacy by ... _________________________________
This design supports users by ... and I know it is inclusive because ... _________________________________
Draw or Plan Here
Sketch the system, tool choice, input, process, and output.
Drawing / planning space — use the full paper packet for a larger workspace.
Role Play or Activity
Team members role play hardware, software, input, output, user, and troubleshooter to explain a system.
Tools Used Today
Digital: Micro Bit, Microsoft MakeCode, Dash robot, Canva, Google Slides, Docs, Sheets, or systems design artifact.
Unplugged: System model cards, network pathway map, troubleshooting protocol, accessibility audit, or privacy and tool choice comparison.

DLCS Studio — Worksheet Packets

Child-Ready Worksheets — All Grades and Units

Open any lesson card in the Curriculum Dashboard and select the Worksheet tab to access the full worksheet for that lesson. Each worksheet includes key vocabulary, sentence starters, drawing space, role play, and tool notes — sized and scaffolded for the grade level.

Worksheet Studio

Use this page as the access point for student ready Word worksheet downloads. Open a lesson card, select the Worksheet tab, then choose Download Word Worksheet. The exported file opens in Microsoft Word and keeps the lesson title, vocabulary, sentence starters, drawing prompt, role play, and tool notes.

Accessibility Focus

Worksheets are scaffolded across the progression. Kindergarten uses drawing and teacher scribing. Grades 1 and 2 add sentence frames. Grades 3 through 5 add planning, evidence, reflection, peer feedback, and project documentation.

How to Use Worksheets
Access from Lesson Cards
Open any lesson in the Curriculum Dashboard, click Open Lesson, then select the Worksheet tab. Each worksheet is fully populated for that lesson.
Word Document Ready
Every lesson worksheet can be exported as a Word document from the Worksheet tab. Use the download button, open the file in Word, and adjust spacing or images for your class context as needed.
Grade K: Visual-First
Kindergarten worksheets are designed for teacher read-aloud, pointing, drawing, and physical manipulation. Sentence starters are oral. Vocabulary is picture-supported.
Grades 4–5: Project-Integrated
Grade 4–5 worksheets connect to the Jobs / Resume / Business Cards project beginning in Unit 2. Students build a cumulative portfolio across the year.
AI Pathway
A developmentally sequenced pathway.
This pathway surfaces the AI lessons embedded across the K to 5 curriculum. Use the AI Only filter inside the curriculum dashboard to see the connected lesson cards.
DLCS Learning Progression Embedded in the Site

From noticing and exploring to designing, testing, and explaining.

The curriculum uses the DLCS progression as an internal design frame. K through 2 lessons emphasize concrete exploration, oral language, safe routines, and guided discovery. Grades 3 through 5 extend those foundations into planning, abstraction, debugging, evidence based explanation, collaboration, and responsible digital creation.

Concrete before abstract

Students begin with stories, manipulatives, movement, drawings, and teacher modeling before they move into formal vocabulary or independent digital production.

Vocabulary in context

Terms such as algorithm, pattern, system, private information, debugging, data, and model appear inside meaningful tasks rather than isolated definitions.

Creation with reflection

Students do not only use tools. They explain choices, test ideas, revise work, and connect their products to a real classroom purpose or audience.

Responsible participation

Computing and society concepts are revisited across the year so safety, privacy, kindness, accessibility, and digital responsibility remain part of every strand.

Scholarly Note

Professional Implementation Note

This curriculum presents a projected sequence and progression for K–5 DLCS instruction. Tap to read the full professional context.

This site presents a projected lesson sequence and developmental progression for K–5 DLCS instruction, together with illustrative examples of instructional resources. All content is intended to inform and support professional practice, not to prescribe a fixed or scripted curriculum. Educators should exercise professional judgment in adapting pacing, activities, station structures, texts, tools, and assessment evidence to their local context. This includes responding to class dynamics, student readiness, accessibility needs, multilingual learner needs, available technologies, district expectations, time constraints, and local priorities. The progression is designed to promote coherent planning while remaining responsive to diverse contexts. All lesson cards and materials are provisional and have been developed in alignment with current disciplinary frameworks and emergent scholarship. Their design and structure reflect an experienced educator’s efforts to organize, access, and implement curricular resources more effectively. All content and design elements will be systematically piloted during the 2026–2027 academic year and iteratively refined through a research-informed review of classroom implementation, student learning outcomes, and contextual factors.
